en: Send your renowned champion and lion!
Behold this might of mine!
Though you fill the earth like the blue sky,
Looming vast as a gorge-riven mountain,
His two eyes bulging,
As though he would suck out any soul he struck,
As though, without a backward glance,
He would slaughter any living being—
Such was Sarybay’s appearance.
His immense weight scorched the earth,
His ferocity scorched the people,
And he began a great upheaval.
The wretch, despairing of life,
Caused many another soul
To perish outright.
Writhing in rage,
The people despaired of their lives,
While divine power struck the madman
With all its force.
Toward Külchoro
He leveled his blue-steel spear.
Before he could arrive ahead of an arrow,
Before he could reach and transfix
The warrior favored by fortune,
His mind crowded with grave fears,
The poor youth beset by many troubles,
The hero Seytek, son of Semetey,
Leveled his spear and charged;
Keeping him from reaching his uncle,
He cast his fly-like life aside.
He too was a falcon and a lion;
His valor and leonine courage
Had now come to the fore.
The playful hero Seytek
Had come out onto the plain
To shield his gray-wolf uncle.
His earliest forefather was Tügöl Khan;
The poor youth’s roots ran deep,
And all his forefathers were khans;
From birth, Kydyr had blessed him.
He was the offspring of my hero.
“That buried swine will reach
My uncle, whose strength is nearly spent,” he thought.
He is the black eye of the demon;
When he strains, he sucks out life,
Calamity incarnate.
Sarybay had turned deadly earnest
And unleashed surpassing fury.
Dust rose everywhere,
And this wretched, faithless world
Seemed utterly overturned.
He lunged in bitter desperation,
Clawing the earth like a polar bear.
Leaning back, he drew his mace,
And when his violent rage seized him,
He seemed capable of shattering the blue sky.
Behold the monstrous Sarybay;
See how his fury raged.
May your renown pass away, cursed raider;
May you die and be laid in the earth.
May your fortunate city be bound,
May you die and be bound beneath the ground.
He advanced, bellowing and snarling,
Clattering in fury,
Making ready like a tiger,
Whose charge none could survive.
He flared up in raging fury,
Changing through countless forms without pause.
He stormed and thundered in wrath,
His towering hair and beard bristling,
As vast as the Üңkür-Koo gorge.
Anyone who entered his reach,
He seemed ready to seize and swallow;
Such was Sarybay’s nature.
Sarybay rode out prepared,
With all his weapons fastened.
Like a returning blast of bitter cold,
Like snow and ice that tormented living souls,
The wretched hero Sarybay,
When you beheld his greatest might,
Was like an icy wind sweeping down the valley.
Raging together with Jelmayan,
He strained as though to swallow and devour,
Lest it be said that he surrendered him to the enemy.
Shall I settle hidden away,
And rather than go on living thus,
Become prey for the blue vulture?
Without coming to my uncle’s aid,
Shall I turn my tulpar’s head away
And stand there drooping,
Like a man struck by palsy?
This raging Sarybay—
I shall reach him from the flank.
My dear uncle,
Let me become your support!”
He lashed Telkyzyl,
And if you ask about the state of that sea-like hero,
Tears streamed from his two eyes
And dripped upon his chest.
His waist arched firmly backward,
And his boiling eyes bulged.
Your ready-born falcon
Whipped Telkyzyl,
And where the mountain vanished at the pass,
He wheeled Telkyzyl’s head.
The sharp steel spear—
Then the hero Seytek
Gripped it crosswise in his hand
And came on, making the earth tremble.
When he reached the warrior,
The infidel hero Sarybay,
He marked the face of the right kidney,
The place beside the backbone,
Thinking, “Here is the surest place to kill,”
And reached the dreadful, venomous infidel,
The warrior Sarybay,
From the flank.
He thrust hard into his kidney as he passed.
But when his spear struck,
The infidel son of the Monster
Proved surpassingly cunning.
Fixing his eye firmly upon the mortal spot,
Seytek unleashed his fiercest fury.
“He has a powerful arm and deadly venom;
He may suddenly thrust straight through.
It would be shameful if I gave no aid.
If my uncle Külchoro closes his eyes,
We shall retreat along the valley.
We shall become a feast for foreign foes,
Then be driven about like sheep
And become the enemy’s banquet.
If my dear uncle perishes,
Who will brandish the black-edged battle-axe
And wield it without faltering?
Who will lead the many Kyrgyz and Argyn
Without plunging them into grief?
Who will whirl the hawthorn-handled battle-axe
And swing it straight and true?
Who will lead the teeming Kyrgyz and Nogoy
Without casting them into turmoil?
If we lose my lion uncle Kül,
We shall retreat along the valley
And be like a fire gone out.
We shall settle along the hillsides
And be like the moon that has set.
If we lose our mane and tail,
We shall be left maimed.
If the head remains but a horn is broken,
We shall be left hornless.
If one of the horns breaks,
We shall be left powerless.
If one breast is severed,
We shall be left without milk.
If death has come, I shall die;
But if fortune favors me, Sarybay,
I shall slash you and spill your blood.
I shall wage a mighty struggle
And rescue my resourceful uncle
From the hands of the wrathful one;
I shall deliver him!”
From birth, the hero Seytek
Was as mighty as half a mountain.
Without resorting to guile, for his uncle,
“I am famished—grant me blood,” he cried.
“My true father, the lion Almambet,
I am afflicted—grant me strength,” he cried.
Against the enraged infidel,
The warrior Khan Sarybay,
To keep him from reaching the hero Seytek,
He readied the steel-shafted spear,
Leveling it straight,
Resolved to die as a sacrifice
Before the hero Seytek.
“My true enemy is Sarybay;
I shall meet him in combat.
To inflict grievous torment,
And rescue the renowned young Seytek
From the mighty demonic infidel,
The warrior son of the Monster,”
He came to deliver him.
When he lashed Kulansur,
The horse revealed his pedigree as a tulpar.
Across sixty defiles and eighty ridges,
He gathered himself into a sweeping stride,
His true tulpar form revealed.
When his hoof struck the black earth,
It split apart in every direction.
From before Sarybay
He flew and bounded like a cloud,
Making the broad common land
Collapse on every side.
The ground he trod burst asunder,
And stones a spear’s length high
Whirled like tents
Above the choro’s head.
Steam poured from his nostrils,
Billowing like smoke from an army.
The earth seemed to end in shimmering haze
As he drew near Sarybay.
The lion choro favored by fortune
Reached the wrathful one,
And thrust the infidel Sarybay
Straight through the collar.
The hero Seytek had staked
His fly-like life upon a hair.
He arrived swifter than an arrow
And struck hard as he passed.
As though he had punched a stone,
The steel spear bent,
And the force bore heavily upon the mighty man.
A white cloud as broad as a house
From Sarybay’s flank
Burst forth, wheeling like a vulture.
The spear that struck so violently
Shattered into eighty pieces.
Among warriors and lions,
Among heroes of uncommon power,
Mane and tail streamed free.
Telkyzyl, driven with all his strength,
Was like a foul blow struck
Against the shinbone;
He plunged into the black earth,
And the lion’s true prowess was revealed.
Before Seytek could recover,
Sarybay, son of the Monster,
Rushed upon the hero Seytek.
Seeking some means to defeat him,
The accursed one found his opening
And prepared to strike with his mace.
He braced himself and gathered strength,
Swaying as though about to strike,
His gorge-like mouth gaping,
The gray foam pouring from his mouth
And scattering across his chest.
Just as he reached him to swing the mace,
Just as he was about to take Seytek’s head,
Külchoro, favored by fortune,
Shouted, “Calamity!”
The gray-wolf servant, deftest of all,
Raised the battle cry, “Manas!”
Drew his scabbardless sword,
And appealed to the spirit
Of the magnanimous hero who had passed into eternity.
Baby, your time is gone.
You have not yet had a fertile bone.
Ten bones, eighty bones,
Full of excitement.
Break the river, build a road,
Attacking the face
You will have a match,
Oh boy, where are you going to go?
It is not a mountain to predict.
The son of the monster disbelieved,
They are not human.
Sarybay, son of a monster
It's hell itself,
